steps.title: Strangers need a shared key
text: Lesson 1 locked data with a shared key. But how do two programs get that key when anyone can listen to the wire?
They use a {{term:key-exchange}}. Each side sends a public piece, and each side combines it with a private piece to reach the same secret.
This lesson runs three exchanges: X25519, ML-KEM, and the two together.
Built to show the parts. Do not copy.

steps.title: Each side makes a private piece
text: The client picks a random private number. It stays on the client, and the secrets panel lists it under the client lane.
From the private number, the client computes a public {{term:key-share}}. It is safe to send the share, because nobody can work back from it to the private number.

steps.title: The public share crosses the wire
text: The share is 32 bytes and it travels in the clear. An eavesdropper sees it.
Try it: switch to the eavesdropper view. Eve sees the shares go by, and her column in the secrets panel stays short.

steps.title: Two sides, one secret
text: Each side now combines its own private number with the other side's public share. Both reach the same 32-byte secret.
Watch the two grids. Cells fill in as each side finishes, and thin lines join the cells when the two values match.

Picture mixing paint. Each side adds a private color to a shared base and sends the mix. Each side then adds its private color to the other's mix. Both end with the same final color. A listener who saw only the mixes cannot split them apart.

claims.text: X25519 gives both sides the same 32-byte shared secret from their own private key and the other side's public key.

steps.title: Check that both sides agree
text: Matching secrets only help when both sides know they match. So each round ends with a confirm message.
The confirm message is a seal made with the new secret. The server checks it, and a wrong secret fails the check.
Try it: swap the server's share for an attacker's share. The two secrets differ, and the confirmation check fails.

steps.title: Why add ML-KEM
text: X25519 is safe today. A large {{term:quantum-computer}} could break it later, and an attacker can record traffic now and wait.
{{term:ml-kem}} rests on different math, and no known quantum method breaks it.
The client sends an encapsulation key of 1,184 bytes. Think of it as an open box that anyone can close but only the client can open.

claims.text: ML-KEM-768 uses a 1,184-byte encapsulation key and a 1,088-byte ciphertext, and no known quantum algorithm breaks it.

steps.title: A damaged box gives no warning
text: The server seals a random secret in a box of 1,088 bytes and sends it back. Only the client's private key opens that box.
A damaged box still opens, but to a different secret, and ML-KEM reports no error. The two sides now disagree and neither one knows yet.
Try it: flip one byte of the box. Only the confirm message catches the difference.

tryIt.label: Flip one byte of the ML-KEM box

claims.text: ML-KEM decapsulation of a modified ciphertext returns a pseudorandom secret instead of an error (implicit rejection).

steps.title: Both at once
text: The {{term:hybrid}} exchange runs X25519 and ML-KEM together. The client share is 1,216 bytes and the server share is 1,120 bytes.
The final secret is 64 bytes: 32 from ML-KEM, then 32 from X25519. An attacker must break both to read the traffic.
This guards against record now, decrypt later. If X25519 falls one day, the ML-KEM half still holds.

claims.text: In the lab, the hybrid secret is 64 bytes, ML-KEM first then X25519, and the shares are 1,216 bytes (client) and 1,120 bytes (server).

steps.title: What the hybrid covers
text: The hybrid protects the key exchange. The certificates that show who the server is stay classical, and lesson 4 covers them.
So an attacker who records a session today cannot read it later. That attacker could still fake a server if the certificate math falls.
Built to show the parts. Do not copy.

claims.text: The hybrid protects the key exchange only. Certificates stay classical.
